messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kofi is a 19-year-old man who works as a detective in a mid-sized city, though he has only been on the force for a few months. The trauma that reshaped his life occurred two years ago, when he was held captive for three days by a group of men who had mistaken him for a witness in a case. They kept him in a basement, bound and blindfolded, and the things he heard during those hours—the scrape of a chair, the murmur of voices planning his fate, the sound of a gun being loaded—have never left him. He was eventually released when the real witness was found, but Kofi came out of that basement a different person.

In the months that followed, Kofi found himself struggling in ways he could not name. He knew exactly what had happened to him, but when his girlfriend or his colleagues asked about it, the words would not come. He could feel the shape of the memory in his chest—the helplessness, the cold concrete against his back—but his mouth would go dry, and he would shake his head, unable to describe it. This frustration only deepened his resolve to push the whole thing out of his mind. He began trying hard not to think about the trauma, telling himself that if he just refused to dwell on it, the feelings would fade. But the memories did not cooperate. Sometimes, without warning, he would be standing in the precinct break room or sitting in his car, and the full emotional intensity of the event would wash over him—the terror, the certainty that he was going to die—even though no image or clear thought accompanied it. He would feel his heart race, his palms sweat, and he would have no idea why. At other times, he would hear things in his head that he had heard during those three days: the creak of a door, a man’s low laugh. These auditory intrusions were the worst, because they felt so real, as if the basement were still around him.

To cope, Kofi developed a set of rigid rules that he followed without question. He stopped going out at night or being outside after dark, because the darkness reminded him of the blindfold and the uncertainty of what might happen next. He also began avoiding any form of physical contact with others—a hand on his shoulder, a pat on the back, even his girlfriend reaching for his hand in bed. Each touch felt like a violation, like hands grabbing him in the dark. He told himself these precautions were just common sense, but they were beginning to cost him. His girlfriend grew distant, hurt by his refusal to let her near him. At work, his partner noticed that Kofi would flinch if someone approached him from behind, and he would always position himself with his back to a wall. Kofi was certain that if he let his guard down, if he stopped controlling his environment, something terrible would happen again. He believed the world was full of people who could take him, and that the only way to stay safe was to stay alert and stay away.

What finally brought Kofi to seek help was a moment at the precinct last week. He was reviewing case files late one evening, and a colleague accidentally dropped a metal filing cabinet drawer. The sound—a sharp, metallic bang—sent Kofi diving under his desk, his heart pounding, his breath coming in short gasps. He stayed there for several minutes, unable to move, while his partner tried to coax him out. After that, his captain told him he needed to see someone, or he would be placed on administrative leave. Kofi agreed, but what he is most afraid of is not losing his job. He is afraid that if he starts talking about what happened, the words will fail him again, and he will be left with nothing but the feelings—the terror, the helplessness, the sounds that will not stop. He hopes, more than anything, that there is a way to make the memories quiet so he can go back to being the person he was before.
